\chapter{The Pair That Proves Grimm's Law}
\label{ch:family}
\hlchaptermodality{16}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can identify close family members in German and say who someone is.}

Four people and two words for groups of them, and a sound law legible across all four. Vater against pater is p becoming f; Mutter against mater is t becoming th and then moving again inside German; Bruder against frater is a breathy b flattening one way in Germanic and turning to f in Latin, so the swap runs the opposite way; and Schwester against soror is the one that did not move at all, because the law touches stops and leaves an s alone. Every word in the chapter is inherited, where every month name was bought.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[der Vater]{der Vater — \textquotedblleft{}father\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C10-vater}



\begin{quote}
The months were bought from Rome. Nothing in this chapter was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der Vater}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der Vater} — \textquotedblleft{}father.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

A \emph{der}-word, two syllables, and the first letter is a trap for an English eye.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{v-as-f} — German \emph{v} is an \textbf{f}. You were given this on \emph{vier}, \textquotedblleft{}four,\textquotedblright{} and it has not changed: \emph{Vater} opens \emph{FAH-}, never \emph{VAH-}.
  \item \texttt{vowel-a-long} — the \emph{a} is long and open, the \emph{ah} of English \emph{father}.
  \item \texttt{r-final} — and it closes on the soft \emph{r} you have been ending words with since \emph{Uhr}.
\end{itemize}

\emph{FAH-ter}. Say it beside English \textbf{father} and the only real difference is the middle consonant.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Vater\textquotedblright{} — FAH-ter
  \item the letter and the sound — \textquotedblleft{}V on the page, f in the mouth\textquotedblright{}
  \item it beside its English twin — \textquotedblleft{}Vater, father\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}der Vater.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}father.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der Vater}.) Which article? (\emph{\textbf{Der}}.) How is the \emph{V} said? (\textbf{As an} \emph{f}.) Which number gave you that? (\emph{\textbf{Vier}}.) Next: why that \emph{f} is there at all.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Vater und pater]{Vater and pater}

\label{lesson:GE-C10-vater-pater}



\begin{quote}
You were given a sound law once, on \emph{Donner} and \emph{thunder}. Here it is again, on the oldest word in the language.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
One ancient word, reconstructed as \emph{*ph\textsubscript{2}tér}, went into every branch of the family. Then the Germanic branch did something the others did not.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{branch} & \textbf{what it did to the first sound} & \textbf{result} \\
\midrule
Latin, and Romance after it & kept the \textbf{p} & \emph{pater}, French \emph{père} \\
Germanic & turned it into an \textbf{f} & \textbf{f}ather, \textbf{V}ater \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The German \emph{V} is an old spelling of that \emph{f}. Take the letter away and the two Germanic words are the same word.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
That \emph{p} $\to$ \emph{f} is one line of Grimm's law, the shift that separated the Germanic languages from the rest. It ran through the whole vocabulary at once, which is why it is a law and not an anecdote.

And it is why German and English \textbf{agree} here while French sits on the other side. They agree because they are on the same side of one ancient change — not because either borrowed from the other. The month names came from Rome. This word never went anywhere.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the two Germanic ones — \textquotedblleft{}Vater, father\textquotedblright{}
  \item the Latin one — \textquotedblleft{}pater\textquotedblright{}
  \item the change — \textquotedblleft{}p became f\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}pater, Vater — p to f.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin keep? (\textbf{The} \emph{p} — \emph{pater}.) What did Germanic do with it? (\textbf{Turned it into an} \emph{f}.) What is that shift called? (\textbf{Grimm's law}.) So why do German and English match? (\textbf{Same side of the change}.) Next: the mother, and the second leg of the same law.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[die Mutter]{die Mutter — \textquotedblleft{}mother\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C10-mutter}



\begin{quote}
The father's first sound changed. This one held.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: die Mutter}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{die Mutter} — \textquotedblleft{}mother.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

A \emph{die}-word beside \emph{der Vater}, and the pair is how the two articles are usually first met in a sentence about people.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{mund-short-u} — the \emph{u} is \textbf{short}, the vowel of English \emph{put}, not the \emph{uh} of English \emph{mother}.
  \item \texttt{d-t-final} — and the \emph{-tt-} is a crisp double \emph{t}.
\end{itemize}

\emph{MOO-ter}, with the \emph{oo} clipped short. Weight on the first syllable, as it is on \emph{Vater}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}die Mutter\textquotedblright{} — MOO-ter, short
  \item the pair with their articles — \textquotedblleft{}der Vater, die Mutter\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English pair — \textquotedblleft{}father, mother\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}der Vater, die Mutter.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}mother.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Die Mutter}.) Which article? (\emph{\textbf{Die}}.) Is the \emph{u} long or short? (\textbf{Short}.) Say both parents together. (\textbf{Der Vater, die Mutter}.) Next: the consonant in the middle, which did move.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Mutter und mater]{Mutter and mater}

\label{lesson:GE-C10-mutter-mater}



\begin{quote}
The father moved at the front. The mother moves in the middle.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
The first sound of this word never changed anywhere: \emph{m} in Latin, \emph{m} in English, \emph{m} in German. The \textbf{middle} one did, twice.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{stage} & \textbf{the middle sound} & \textbf{word} \\
\midrule
Latin, untouched & \textbf{t} & \emph{mater}, French \emph{mère} \\
Germanic, first shift & \textbf{th} & mo\textbf{th}er \\
German, its own later shift & \textbf{tt} & Mu\textbf{tt}er \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English stopped after one change. German kept going and ran a second shift of its own, which is why \emph{mother} and \emph{Mutter} differ where \emph{father} and \emph{Vater} barely do.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Two shifts, one after the other, both of them laws rather than accidents. The first separated Germanic from Latin; the second separated German from English.

So the distance between any two of these words is a count of how many shifts have run between them. \emph{Mater} to \emph{mother} is one. \emph{Mother} to \emph{Mutter} is one more. That is the whole reason the family looks scattered from the outside and is perfectly orderly from the inside.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three in order — \textquotedblleft{}mater, mother, Mutter\textquotedblright{}
  \item the middle sound each time — \textquotedblleft{}t, th, tt\textquotedblright{}
  \item what never changed — \textquotedblleft{}the m\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}mater, mother, Mutter.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the Latin? (\emph{\textbf{Mater}}.) What did the first shift make of the middle \emph{t}? (\emph{\textbf{Th}}.) And the second? (\textbf{The} \emph{tt} \textbf{of} \emph{Mutter}.) How many shifts separate \emph{mater} from \emph{Mutter}? (\textbf{Two}.) Next: the word for both of them at once.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[die Eltern]{die Eltern — \textquotedblleft{}parents\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C10-eltern}



\begin{quote}
You have a father and a mother. German has one word for the two of them, and it only comes in the plural.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: die Eltern}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{die Eltern} — \textquotedblleft{}parents.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

It takes \emph{die}, like every plural you have met, and there is no singular form of it. You cannot say \textquotedblleft{}one \emph{Eltern}\textquotedblright{}; a single one is \emph{der Vater} or \emph{die Mutter}.

Underneath, it is a \textbf{comparative} that hardened into a noun: it means \textquotedblleft{}the \textbf{older} ones.\textquotedblright{} English had the same formation and kept it as \textbf{elders}, narrowed to people of standing rather than to the two who raised you.

\begin{culture}
Every word in this chapter is inherited. Not one of them was bought.

That is not an accident of this list. The words a language uses every hour of every day are the ones an incoming language cannot displace, and there is nothing more everyday than the people in a house. Rome ran the calendar, so German took the calendar's words. Rome did not run anybody's family.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}die Eltern\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two it stands for — \textquotedblleft{}der Vater, die Mutter\textquotedblright{}
  \item what it literally means — \textquotedblleft{}the older ones\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English word from the same formation — \textquotedblleft{}elders\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}die Eltern.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}parents.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Die Eltern}.) What is the singular? (\textbf{There is none} — use \emph{der Vater} or \emph{die Mutter}.) What does it mean underneath? (\textbf{The older ones}.) Was any word in this chapter borrowed? (\textbf{No} — all inherited.) Next: the brother.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der Bruder]{der Bruder — \textquotedblleft{}brother\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C10-bruder}



\begin{quote}
Out of the parents and into their children. This one you can almost read already.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der Bruder}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der Bruder} — \textquotedblleft{}brother.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

A \emph{der}-word. Set it beside English \textbf{brother} and one vowel is the whole distance: \emph{oo} where English has \emph{uh}.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-u-long} — a long \emph{oo}, as in English \emph{food}.
  \item \texttt{r-uvular} — the \emph{r} after \emph{B} is made at the back of the throat, a light scrape rather than a roll.
  \item \texttt{r-final} — and the ending is the soft closing \emph{r} again.
\end{itemize}

\emph{BROO-der}, weight on the first, exactly the rhythm of \emph{Vater} and \emph{Mutter}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Bruder\textquotedblright{} — BROO-der
  \item the English twin — \textquotedblleft{}Bruder, brother\textquotedblright{}
  \item three of the family so far — \textquotedblleft{}der Vater, die Mutter, der Bruder\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}der Bruder.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}brother.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der Bruder}.) Which article? (\emph{\textbf{Der}}.) Long or short \emph{u}? (\textbf{Long} — \emph{BROO}.) Next: what Latin did to the front of it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Bruder und frater]{Bruder and frater}

\label{lesson:GE-C10-bruder-frater}



\begin{quote}
On the father, Latin had the \emph{p} and Germanic had the \emph{f}. Here it is the other way round, and that is not a contradiction.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
The ancient word is reconstructed as \emph{*b\textsuperscript{h}réh\textsubscript{2}tēr} — it begins with a \textbf{breathy b}, a sound neither language kept.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{branch} & \textbf{what it did with the breathy b} & \textbf{result} \\
\midrule
Latin & turned it into an \textbf{f} & \emph{frater}, French \emph{frère} \\
Germanic & flattened it to a plain \textbf{b} & \textbf{b}rother, \textbf{B}ruder \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \emph{Bruder} and \emph{frater} really are one word, and the \emph{b} against the \emph{f} is the mark of which branch you are standing in.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
It looks reversed against \emph{Vater} and \emph{pater}, where Germanic held the \emph{f}. It is not. The two words started from \textbf{different ancient sounds}: a plain \emph{p} in one, a breathy \emph{b} in the other. Grimm's law moved each of them once, in its own direction, and the results cross over.

That is what makes it a law worth the name. It does not say \textquotedblleft{}Germanic prefers \emph{f}.\textquotedblright{} It says each old sound goes to one particular new one, every time — and you can run it forwards on a word you have never seen.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}frater, Bruder\textquotedblright{}
  \item which branch has which — \textquotedblleft{}Latin f, Germanic b\textquotedblright{}
  \item the father pair beside it — \textquotedblleft{}pater, Vater\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}frater, Bruder.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the Latin for \emph{Bruder}? (\emph{\textbf{Frater}}.) Which branch has the \emph{b}? (\textbf{Germanic}.) Does that contradict \emph{pater} and \emph{Vater}? (\textbf{No} — they started from different old sounds.) Next: a cluster of three letters that says two sounds.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[schw-]{schw- — three letters, two sounds}

\label{lesson:GE-C10-schw}



\begin{quote}
One sound cluster before the next word, because the word is unreadable without it.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{sch-sh} — \textbf{sch} is \textbf{one} sound, and it is the \emph{sh} of English \emph{ship}. Not \emph{s-k-h}, not \emph{sk}. Three letters, one consonant.
  \item \texttt{w-as-v} — and German \emph{w} is a \textbf{v}, the rule you were given on \emph{Winter}.
  \item \texttt{schw-cluster} — put them together and \emph{schw-} comes out \textbf{shv-}.
\end{itemize}

English can say \emph{sh} and English can say \emph{v}, but it never puts them side by side at the start of a word. Say \emph{shhh}, hold it, then let it fall straight into \emph{v} without a vowel between: \emph{shv}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the first sound alone — \textquotedblleft{}sh\textquotedblright{}
  \item the second alone — \textquotedblleft{}v\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two joined, no vowel — \textquotedblleft{}shv\textquotedblright{}
  \item it again, slower — \textquotedblleft{}shv\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}shv.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many sounds is \emph{sch}? (\textbf{One} — English \emph{sh}.) How is German \emph{w} said? (\textbf{As a} \emph{v}.) So what does \emph{schw-} sound like? (\emph{\textbf{Shv-}}.) Is there a vowel between them? (\textbf{No}.) Next: the word that starts with it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[die Schwester]{die Schwester — \textquotedblleft{}sister\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C10-schwester}



\begin{quote}
You have the cluster. Here is the word it was for.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: die Schwester}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{die Schwester} — \textquotedblleft{}sister.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\emph{SHVES-ter}. A \emph{die}-word, and the counterpart of \emph{der Bruder}.

On the page it looks unrelated to \textbf{sister}. In the mouth it is not: take the \emph{shv} back to a plain \emph{s} and what is left — \emph{s-e-s-t-e-r} — is the English word with one vowel moved.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{schw-cluster} — \emph{shv-}, straight into the vowel.
  \item \texttt{herz-short-e} — a short open \emph{e}, the vowel of English \emph{bed}.
  \item \texttt{r-final} — and the same soft ending as \emph{Vater}, \emph{Mutter} and \emph{Bruder}.
\end{itemize}

Four family words now, and all four end the same way.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}die Schwester\textquotedblright{} — SHVES-ter
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}der Bruder, die Schwester\textquotedblright{}
  \item all four — \textquotedblleft{}der Vater, die Mutter, der Bruder, die Schwester\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}die Schwester.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}sister.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Die Schwester}.) How does it start? (\emph{\textbf{Shv-}}.) Which article? (\emph{\textbf{Die}}.) Say the brother beside it. (\emph{\textbf{Der Bruder}}.) Next: what Latin did with the same word.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Schwester und soror]{Schwester and soror}

\label{lesson:GE-C10-schwester-soror}



\begin{quote}
The brother's first sound split the two branches. The sister's did not split anything.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
The ancient word is reconstructed as \emph{*swésōr}, and all three descendants keep its \textbf{s}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{the word} & \textbf{the first sound} \\
\midrule
German & \emph{Schwester} & \emph{sch} is a later German dressing on an \textbf{s} \\
English & \emph{sister} & plain \textbf{s} \\
Latin & \emph{soror} & plain \textbf{s} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Grimm's law had nothing to do to an \emph{s}. It moved the stops — the \emph{p}s, \emph{t}s and \emph{b}s — and left this one where it stood, which is why the sister is the one family word whose front sound matches across the whole family.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Latin \emph{soror} is behind French \emph{sœur}, and behind English \textbf{sorority} — which English borrowed back from Latin centuries after it already had \emph{sister} from the same root. The two came in by different doors and nobody noticed they were relatives.

That is the ordinary condition of a big vocabulary: the same ancient word arriving twice, once inherited and once bought, sitting in the dictionary without recognising each other.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three — \textquotedblleft{}Schwester, sister, soror\textquotedblright{}
  \item what they share — \textquotedblleft{}the s\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English word borrowed back from Latin — \textquotedblleft{}sorority\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Schwester, sister, soror.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the Latin? (\emph{\textbf{Soror}}.) What do all three share? (\textbf{The} \emph{s}.) Why did Grimm's law leave it? (\textbf{It moved stops, not} \emph{s}.) What is the \emph{sch} then? (\textbf{Later German dressing on the same} \emph{s}.) Next: the word English does not have.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[die Geschwister]{die Geschwister — \textquotedblleft{}siblings\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C10-geschwister-wort}



\begin{quote}
German has one word for the brother and the sister together. English has \emph{siblings}, which almost nobody says at a kitchen table.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: die Geschwister}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{die Geschwister} — \textquotedblleft{}siblings,\textquotedblright{} brothers and sisters as a set.
\end{quote}

Consider what is inside it. Take off the \emph{Ge-} at the front and \emph{-schwister} is \emph{Schwester}, which you own — the same \emph{shv}, the same ending. A plural, so \emph{die}, and like \emph{Eltern} it has no singular.

\begin{culture}
The odd part is that a word built on \emph{Schwester} covers the \textbf{brothers} too. Two boys and no girls in a house are still \emph{die Geschwister}.

German built the collective on the word that happened to be there, and the collective then outranked the piece it was made from. English never built one at all: it says \emph{brothers and sisters} and reaches for the Latin-derived \emph{siblings} when it needs a single term.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}die Geschwister\textquotedblright{}
  \item the word inside it — \textquotedblleft{}Schwester\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two it covers — \textquotedblleft{}der Bruder, die Schwester\textquotedblright{}
  \item what English says instead — \textquotedblleft{}brothers and sisters\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}die Geschwister.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}siblings.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Die Geschwister}.) Which word is inside it? (\emph{\textbf{Schwester}}.) Does it cover brothers? (\textbf{Yes} — all of them.) Is there a singular? (\textbf{No}.) Next: what that \emph{Ge-} on the front is doing.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[das sammelnde Ge-]{The gathering Ge-}

\label{lesson:GE-C10-ge-kollektiv}



\begin{quote}
One prefix, one job, and the last word showed you it working.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one member in, a whole set out}]
Put \textbf{Ge-} on the front of a word for one member of something, and you get a word for \textbf{the whole set of them}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{in} & \textbf{out} \\
\midrule
\emph{Schwester}, one member & \emph{Geschwister}, the set \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is the machine. It is old, it is Germanic, and German still runs it: a mountain becomes a mountain range, a piece of luggage becomes the luggage, a vegetable becomes the vegetables — each one a bare noun with \emph{Ge-} welded on.

English had this prefix and wore it away to nothing. What is left of it in English are fossils nobody parses any more.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Both plural-only family words in this chapter are made rather than borrowed, and each is made a different way.

\emph{Eltern} takes an adjective and freezes it: \textbf{the older ones}. \emph{Geschwister} takes a noun and gathers it: \textbf{the set of them}.

Neither has a singular, because neither was ever about one person. They name a group directly, and German got both of them out of parts it already had.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item what the prefix does — \textquotedblleft{}one member in, the set out\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair it made — \textquotedblleft{}Schwester, Geschwister\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two plural-only words — \textquotedblleft{}die Eltern, die Geschwister\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Schwester, Geschwister.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the gathering \emph{Ge-} do? (\textbf{Makes a set out of one member}.) Which word in this chapter was built with it? (\emph{\textbf{Geschwister}}.) And how was \emph{Eltern} built instead? (\textbf{From a comparative — the older ones}.) Do either of them have a singular? (\textbf{No}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — the household, and the law that runs through it}

\label{lesson:GE-C10-geschwister}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Four people, two words for groups of them, and one sound law with three lines.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the four, and their two collectives}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{one person} & \textbf{the set they belong to} \\
\midrule
\emph{der Vater} & \emph{die Eltern} \\
\emph{die Mutter} & \emph{die Eltern} \\
\emph{der Bruder} & \emph{die Geschwister} \\
\emph{die Schwester} & \emph{die Geschwister} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both collectives take \emph{die} and neither has a singular. One was frozen out of a comparative, the other gathered with a prefix.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Set the four against their Latin cousins and the law is legible in a line:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{\textbf{Vater}} against \emph{pater} — the \textbf{p} became an \textbf{f}.
  \item \emph{\textbf{Mutter}} against \emph{mater} — the \textbf{t} became \textbf{th}, and then German moved it again.
  \item \emph{\textbf{Bruder}} against \emph{frater} — a breathy \textbf{b} flattened one way in Germanic and turned to \textbf{f} in Latin, so the swap runs the opposite way.
  \item \emph{\textbf{Schwester}} against \emph{soror} — nothing moved. The law does not touch an \textbf{s}.
\end{itemize}

Three moved and one did not, and which is which was decided by the sound, not by the word. That is what makes it predictable.
\end{culture}

\begin{culture}
And every word here is \textbf{inherited}. Not one was bought, where every month name was.

The pattern holds across the whole book: the words a language uses every hour resist replacement, and the words that arrive with an institution come in whole. A calendar is an institution. A household is not.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four with their articles — \textquotedblleft{}der Vater, die Mutter, der Bruder, die Schwester\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two collectives — \textquotedblleft{}die Eltern, die Geschwister\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one that starts shv — \textquotedblleft{}die Schwester\textquotedblright{}
  \item each pair against its Latin — \textquotedblleft{}Vater, pater; Mutter, mater; Bruder, frater; Schwester, soror\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one Latin word that did not move — \textquotedblleft{}soror\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}der Vater, die Mutter, der Bruder, die Schwester.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name the four. (\textbf{Der Vater, die Mutter, der Bruder, die Schwester}.) The word for the two older ones? (\emph{\textbf{Die Eltern}}.) For the two younger? (\emph{\textbf{Die Geschwister}}.) Which of the four is unchanged from Latin at the front? (\emph{\textbf{Schwester}} — the \emph{s} never moved.) And how many of these words did German borrow? (\textbf{None}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
